reviews.review:
honestly not as bad as it looks , at all

i played it all the way solo , Redfall functions like far cry clone on a smaller scale with borderlands loot system , the reason why its bashed so hardly is due to expectations from Arkane , thats it.

if you are looking for a small open world FPS game with a good gunplay that doesn't take 40+ hours to complete , this should be worth a pick up when its 10$ or so.

Rumor has it even the developers hoped Redfall would be canceled after Microsoft acquired Arkane.  It might have been an average L4D knockoff had it been released a decade earlier while Everything Was Vampires but somehow still ended up being kicked out the door unfinished.  It's a looter with no reason to loot (why? There is no crafting!) and a shooter with very poor AI and gunplay.  It couldn't decide whether to be a live service cult-stomping power fantasy or a coop grind or a single player narrative experience with a storyline straight out of mid 2000s True Blood, complete with over-the-top southern accent narration.  I commend the developers for fixing the performance issues and overhauling progression after the game was dead and studio shutdown had been announced but I have to wonder if the effort was worth it.  I am determined to beat Redfall because I paid for it and will likely end up with dozens of hours played, but I do not recommend buying this objectively bad game.

It's been some time since the terrible launch and I wanted to see if it was worth playing now that it's gotten some updates. I bought it at a heavily discounted price, so I figured why not. After booting it the main menu, I was given the options to "Enter" to enter Redfall, or "Esc" to leave Redfall. Deciding that, since i had downloaded the game, I wanted to play Redfall, I hit enter. A "Connecting to server" window popped up, and a "Updated Bethesda agreement" window popped up. the only window I could interact with was the "Connecting to server" window. If I hit cancel, I go back to the main menu. But to connect to the server, I have to agree to the agreement. Which I can't do because I'm connecting to the server. I have never seen a more blatant sign from a higher power that i should not play this game.

Heed my warning, fair Adventurer. Do not buy.

This game had an amazing signature Arkane style, a really cool horror-esque setting, an interesting story, and a solid core gameplay idea that could be boiled down to "Far Cry with vampires", but greedy executives screwed everything up by forcing devs to release a half-baked product while trying to follow modern trends for soulless live service games. 
I bought this game on sale after they patched everything they could, and after the utter disappointment that is Borderlands 4, Redfall feels like a fun walk among the ruins of what could've been amazing.

Redfall, developed by Arkane Austin and published by Bethesda Softworks, is a game built on a premise that should have been a genre standout: an open-world vampire shooter set in a mist-covered Massachusetts island town cut off from the rest of the world. The sun has been blotted out, the tides have frozen in place, and supernatural predators stalk abandoned streets. As one of four survivors — each with their own powers and personality — you set out to unravel the mystery behind the town’s downfall and push back against the vampiric forces tightening their grip. On paper, it reads like a compelling combination of Arkane’s atmospheric storytelling and a more action-oriented co-op shooter structure. And in its earliest moments, Redfall occasionally hints at what that game could have been.

The four playable heroes offer a nice conceptual variety: a telekinetic student, a gadget-driven inventor, a marksman with a spectral companion, and a cryptozoologist with arcane abilities. Their powers complement one another well in theory, creating opportunities for synergy in co-op play and allowing different approaches in solo runs. The town of Redfall itself also has a strong sense of identity. Quaint colonial houses, eerie farmland, vampire-controlled safehouses, cultist-infested streets, and unnervingly quiet waterfronts set the stage for encounters that combine looter-shooter mechanics with occasional touches of supernatural horror. At its rare best, the game achieves small moments of tension—creeping into a flickering house while listening for whispers, or stumbling across a vampire nest that warps local reality.

Combat follows familiar first-person shooter rhythms blended with light RPG elements. Weapons come in tiers, each offering bonuses or traits, and vampires must be weakened before a stake, UV blast, or fire finishes them off. Abilities provide extra mobility, defensive tools, or offensive surges. When players coordinate these tools successfully, fights can feel energetic and chaotic in a fun way. The game supports full co-op, and playing with friends unquestionably improves the pacing by adding layers of strategy and broader firepower. Even basic enemy encounters become more dynamic when teamwork enters the equation.

But while Redfall’s foundations are structurally sound, the execution frequently struggles to match the ambition. One of its most persistent issues is the emptiness of the open world. Despite the atmospheric setting, large sections of the map feel devoid of life, interactivity, or meaningful encounters. Many buildings exist as hollow set pieces, and stretches of the town have little to do beyond moving from objective to objective. What should feel like a breathing, terrified community instead comes across as static and underpopulated, weakening the immersion and removing much of the tension a vampire takeover should evoke.

Enemy behavior also contributes to this lack of engagement. Human cultists and vampire foes alike often display rudimentary or erratic AI, which diminishes both challenge and atmosphere. Rather than stalking, flanking, or overwhelming players in clever ways, many enemies simply run forward or stand in place, making combat too predictable. The game introduces elite vampire types, but their rarity — combined with the flatness of ordinary encounters — reduces the stakes that should define a supernatural shooter. As players advance, especially with powerful loot, the combat loop begins to lose urgency and variety.

Narratively, Redfall never fully capitalizes on its intriguing setup. Much of the story is conveyed through static images and exposition rather than dynamic sequences or environmental storytelling of the kind Arkane is known for. The central villains — the so-called Vampire Gods — are conceptually fascinating but underdeveloped, leaving major threads feeling unresolved or detached. Even the heroes, though distinct in personality, rarely interact meaningfully during missions, which becomes especially noticeable in co-op. As a result, the story feels more like a loose framework for missions than a driving emotional arc.

Technical issues further complicate the experience. At launch and even beyond, players encountered inconsistent performance, odd animations, texture pop-in, hit detection quirks, and a general lack of polish. While patches have improved some aspects, the impression remains that the game arrived in an unfinished state. These problems don’t make Redfall unplayable, but they exacerbate its already uneven pacing and presentation.

Co-op progression design is another misstep. Only the host of a session receives full campaign progression, meaning friends who join must replay missions again later if they want credit in their own worlds. This choice undermines the cooperative fantasy the game heavily advertises and discourages spontaneous drop-in play. Combined with the lack of enemy scaling tuned for groups, co-op can alternate between being trivially easy and oddly chaotic.

In the end, Redfall is a game full of potential that flickers intermittently but never fully ignites. There are fragments of an atmospheric supernatural shooter scattered throughout its world — an abandoned house filled with cult paraphernalia, a silent lighthouse overlooking a blood-red sea, a tense fight inside a warped vampire nest — but these moments are isolated rather than foundational. The overall experience feels stretched thin, with world design, AI, narrative depth, and technical performance all falling short of the ambitions driving the project.

Players who enjoy light looter-shooter mechanics, casual co-op play, or simply exploring eerie environments with friends may still find pockets of enjoyment. But those seeking a polished, narratively rich, or mechanically sharp experience — especially given Arkane’s pedigree — may walk away disappointed. Redfall is a game that aimed for a unique blend of Arkane-style immersion and co-op action but struggled to harmonize its parts, ultimately delivering something intriguing yet unrefined.

Rating: 5/10
